title: Casamance Mangrove Oysters, Grilled and Sun-Dried
author: Compiled from M.C. Cormier-Salem (ORSTOM, May 1987) with Slow Food Ark of Taste and FAO / Slow Food
desc: Mangrove oysters piled with wood in alternate layers 1.5 to 2 m high and burned, removed as they open, then sun-dried two days — the Diola women’s preservation of the Casamance oyster, documented without quantities.
longDesc: The Casamance mangrove oyster is gathered by Diola women on the falling tide. ORSTOM’s 1987 study records the preservation routes: oysters detached from burned branches or roasted or boiled in a large basin, shells opened and the flesh removed (the text notes fingers get burned), then sun-dried 1 to 2 days, or smoked 1 to 2 days on a round tray over the fire, or grilled. For the grill, oysters and wood are stacked in alternate layers until the pile is 1.5 to 2 metres high, the fire is lit and the oysters are removed as they open — undercooked ones go back — and the grilled oysters are sun-dried for two days. Dried flesh is one tenth of the initial weight. The Slow Food Ark of Taste records that in high season the oysters are boiled or grilled and served with pepper sauce and rice, in low season sun-dried, smoked or eaten dried. THE SOURCES PRINT NO QUANTITIES, NO TEMPERATURES AND NO SAFETY FIGURES. This is a documented traditional practice, not a home recipe.
ingredients: Mangrove oysters — gathered at minimum size over 7 cm (ORSTOM); no quantity
Wood for the grilling pile — no quantity
Pepper sauce and rice to serve (Slow Food Ark of Taste) — no quantities
equipment: Baskets or jute sacks for storing
steps: Gather the oysters on the falling tide and keep only those over about 7 cm.
Stack the oysters and wood in alternate layers until the pile is 1.5 to 2 metres high. Light the fire. Remove the oysters from the fire as they open; put the ones that have not opened back.
Open the shells and take out the flesh. Sun-dry the grilled oysters for 2 days (smoked oysters are dried first, then smoked 1 to 2 days; plain sun-drying is 1 to 2 days).
Store in baskets or jute sacks hung above the fire or on rice-granary shelves.
chefTips: The one doneness cue is that oysters are taken off the fire ‘as they open’ (« au fur et à mesure qu’ils s’ouvrent »); undercooked ones are put back.
Dried flesh weighs about a tenth of the starting weight (attributed to DOPM).
Women ‘know how to recognise the state of maturity of the oysters’; no criteria are printed.
commonMistakes: Eating oysters that have not opened on the fire.
Treating the process as a home protocol: no temperature, time-at-temperature or safety limit is published.
servedWith: Pepper sauce and rice (Slow Food Ark of Taste)
storage: In baskets or jute sacks, above the fire or on rice-granary shelves; no storage time is printed.
healthBenefits: A concentrated protein and mineral source when dried.
culturalNote: The practice is the Diola women’s: ORSTOM’s own title assigns it to the ‘système d’exploitation diola’ and the Slow Food Ark of Taste puts some 4,000 Diola women in the annual harvest. The sources describe a harvest that damages mangrove reproduction when branches are cut and a sustainable alternative of wooden frames and strings (strings removed after 5 months), a divergence from the FAO / Slow Food Tobor project (garlands moved at 1.5 months, ready in 4 to 5 months) that is recorded and not merged.
sources: Primary: Cormier-Salem, M.C. (ORSTOM, Géographe), ‘La cueillette des huîtres en Casamance : place de cette pratique dans le système d’exploitation diola’, CRODT/ISRA Dakar, May 1987 (the page header OCR-garbles the year to ‘1981’). TWO-PASS, line-level agreement. Quoted: ‘Le séchage dure 1 à 2 jours, deux jours dans le Bandial où les huîtres ne sont pas fumées, un jour dans le Blouf’; ‘Le fumage dure 1 à 2 jours’; grilling stack ‘jusqu’à obtenir un tas de 1 m50 à 2 m de hauteur’; grilled oysters sun-dried ‘pendant deux jours’; ‘Taille toujours supérieure à 7 cm’.

Second reading: Slow Food Foundation, Ark of Taste, ‘Mangrove Swamp Oyster from Casamance’ — no byline and no date printed (metadata modified 2020-04-16); used only as a corroborating institutional reading. Third: FAO / Slow Food ‘de la terre à la table’ (Tobor project; no date).

No temperature appears anywhere in the ORSTOM source. The prep, rest and cook times above (60 min, 2 days, 60 min) take the printed two-day drying and are otherwise scheduling estimates; the yield of 6 is a scheduling placeholder. A line of ORSTOM’s text refers to a forked stick with a name that the OCR renders unreadably; no reconstruction is offered.
Divergence kept unreconciled: Ark of Taste string removal at 5 months vs FAO / Slow Food readiness at 4 to 5 months and garlands moved at 1.5 months — different projects and sites.
